planting.note: Plant divisions or potted stock as soon as soil can be worked; this scree-dweller resents root disturbance once established.

directions: Native to screes and rocky ledges of the European Alps and Dolomites, this mat-forming cinquefoil hugs the ground with tight rosettes of silvery, silky leaves. In early to midsummer it opens pale to deep pink five-petaled flowers held just above the foliage mat. Plant in sharply drained, gritty or rocky soil in full sun, as it is intolerant of winter wet at the crown. Suits a trough, scree bed, or raised alpine bed rather than a conventional border.

planting.note: Start seed indoors in late winter or sow direct once frost danger has passed; self-sows readily once established.

directions: Found on open Himalayan slopes from Afghanistan to Nepal, this cinquefoil forms clumps of deeply cut leaves densely covered in silvery hairs, giving the foliage a shimmering silver cast. Golden-yellow flowers with a darker eye appear on branching stems from early to late summer, and some wild populations show coppery-orange or red-flushed petals. Grow in well-drained garden soil in full sun; it tolerates poor, stony ground and benefits from division every few years to maintain vigor. Deadhead spent flower stalks to encourage repeat bloom.

planting.note: Seed benefits from a cold, moist stratification period before sowing, mimicking its subalpine and arctic-alpine habitat.

directions: Circumboreal in distribution, this low cinquefoil grows wild on alpine turf, limestone outcrops, and arctic tundra across Europe and North America. It forms tufted rosettes of palmate, five- to seven-lobed leaves and bears bright golden-yellow flowers, usually with a small orange basal spot, from late spring through summer. Grow in lean, gritty, well-drained soil in full sun; it is naturally adapted to short growing seasons and thin alpine soils and dislikes rich garden beds. Well suited to rock gardens, scree, or alpine troughs.

planting.note: Divide established clumps in early spring or plant container stock once soil is workable.

directions: Native to dry grassy steppe and hillsides from southeastern Europe through the Caucasus and Central Asia, this cranesbill forms an upright, airy clump of finely divided leaves. Pale lilac-pink flowers with darker veining open in loose branching clusters from early to midsummer, standing well above the foliage. It is one of the parent species behind the well-known hybrid Geranium 'Nimbus', valued here for its own wiry, drought-tolerant constitution. Grow in average to lean, well-drained soil in full sun, and cut back after flowering to refresh the foliage.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring; established clumps also transplant well in early fall.

directions: Native to woodland margins and meadows of the Caucasus mountains, this cranesbill forms a dense mound of broad, softly hairy, lobed leaves. Large violet-blue flowers veined in deeper purple cover the plant in early summer, and this species is one of the two Caucasian parents of the popular garden hybrid Geranium x magnificum. Grow in humus-rich, moisture-retentive soil in partial sun to light shade, where it makes reliable, long-lived ground cover. Shear lightly after the first flush to tidy foliage and may prompt sparse rebloom.

planting.note: Plant divisions or potted stock in spring once hard frosts have passed.

directions: Native to Siberia, Mongolia, and northeastern China, this cranesbill is prized as much for its foliage as its flowers. Soft, grayish-green, velvety leaves emerge in spring and turn rich shades of red, orange, and purple in autumn, well before most hardy geraniums color up. Violet-purple flowers with a darker central zone appear over a long season from early summer into fall. Grow in moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun, where it tolerates cooler summers better than many Mediterranean geranium species.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring; semi-ripe cuttings are typically rooted in late summer by growers.

directions: Native to the mountains of western China, this slow-growing evergreen shrub gets its common name from the small wart-like bumps covering its young stems. Glossy dark green leaves with spiny, white-backed undersides clothe an arching, mounded form, and golden-yellow flowers in spring are followed by blue-black berries in fall. Grow in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; once established it tolerates drought and poor soil far better than many broadleaf evergreens. Its dense, prickly habit also makes it useful as a low barrier planting.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring; nursery stock is typically propagated from semi-ripe cuttings.

directions: Native to the Hubei region of central China, this compact evergreen shrub forms a dense, rounded mound of small, spiny, dark green leaves with a strikingly white, chalky underside that flashes in the wind. Solitary golden-yellow flowers in late spring give way to small blue-black berries. Grow in well-drained soil in full sun for the best foliage contrast and most compact habit; it also tolerates partial shade but grows looser. This species has been used as a parent of several popular compact evergreen barberry hybrids.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring; stock is typically produced from semi-ripe cuttings or collected seed.

directions: Collected originally from high-altitude scrub in southeastern Tibet, this deciduous barberry is grown chiefly for its striking powdery, glaucous-blue young stems and similarly blue-toned oval leaves. Pale yellow flowers in spring are followed by oval red berries that persist after the blue-gray foliage colors and drops in autumn. Grow in well-drained soil in full sun, where the strongest sun exposure brings out the most intense blue-white bloom on the bark. It makes a striking winter specimen once the leaves fall and the colored stems are exposed.
